data.text: The natural walking model is intended to provide a realistic walking experience and produce the perception of movement, but it does not provide experience optimization and can only be used to enhance presence. Optimization can be achieved by using the natural walking model to control exposure duration and address cybersickness. Since cybersickness symptoms rise proportionally with session duration, shorter exposure durations can help eliminate or at least minimize these symptoms.
points: The natural walking model is intended to provide a realistic walking experience and produce the perception of movement.
The natural walking model does not provide experience optimization and can only be used to enhance presence.
Optimization can be achieved by using the natural walking model to control exposure duration and address cybersickness.
Shorter exposure durations can help eliminate or at least minimize cybersickness because symptoms rise proportionally with session duration.

data.text: VR exposure duration depends on world size, travel speed, travel time, and interaction time. While techniques like teleportation or terrain modification can reduce exposure, they may compromise realism or the user's mental map. Semi-interactive tours can limit interaction time by using system-controlled navigation and restricting interaction to a specific set of objects at points of interest.
points: VR exposure duration depends on world size, travel speed, travel time, and interaction time.
Teleportation and higher travel speeds can reduce exposure time but may compromise realism and naturalness.
Modifying terrain and point-of-interest distances can reduce travel time but may hamper the user's mental map and perception of space.
Semi-interactive tours use system-controlled navigation to limit interaction time to a small set of objects at specific points of interest.

data.text: In a semi-interactive virtual reality (VR) tour, interaction time at each point of interest (POI) can be limited to force the user to move. Exposure duration can be optimized by finding an optimum path that either minimizes the total navigation and interaction time for all POIs or maximizes the number of POIs experienced within a fixed time limit. Optimizing exposure duration is expected to optimize the prevalence and onset of cybersickness because exposure duration and cybersickness are directly related.
points: Interaction time at each point of interest (POI) can be limited to force movement.
Exposure duration can be optimized by either minimizing time for all POIs or maximizing the number of POIs within a fixed time.
Optimizing exposure duration is expected to optimize cybersickness because exposure duration and cybersickness are directly related.

data.text: The virtual world is represented as a weighted graph where points of interest are vertices and edges represent paths between them. Edge weights are assigned based on Euclidean distance, meaning the graph does not have to be complete. The objective is to find a path that covers all POIs in the least possible time while maintaining a realistic speed.
points: The virtual world is represented as a weighted graph where points of interest (POIs) are vertices and edges represent paths.
The graph does not need to be complete because there may not always be a direct path between certain POIs.
Edge weights are assigned as Euclidean distances for connected POIs and infinity for those that are not directly connected.
Each point of interest is a node, while a single structure may contain multiple nodes.
The goal is to find a path covering all POIs in the shortest time while maintaining a realistic speed.

data.text: The travel-time algorithm computes the time between connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model, where perceived speed is 2.1 times the actual speed. The total travel time is derived from the integral of the distance element divided by the perceived speed. This result is simplified into a travel-time estimate tau D that uses a constant V naught based on the user's height.
points: Compute the travel time between directly connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model.
Perceived instantaneous walking speed is the actual walking speed multiplied by a visual gain of 2.1.
The total travel time is the integral of the distance element divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous walking speed.
The simplified travel-time estimate tau D is calculated using distance D, a constant V naught, and a Fourier-series expansion.
The constant V naught is determined by the user's height.

data.text: The total travel time for a path is the sum of the Euclidean distances between consecutive vertices. Minimizing the time to visit all vertices is a variation of the travelling salesman problem. Because the graph may not be complete, hypothetical edges are introduced between unconnected vertices using the shortest path lengths. These hypothetical weights are well-defined because the graph is connected.
points: The total travel time for a path is the sum of the Euclidean distances between consecutive vertices.
Minimizing the total travel time to visit all vertices is a variation of the travelling salesman problem.
The graph may not be complete, which means it might not have a Hamiltonian path.
Hypothetical edges are introduced between unconnected vertices using the shortest path lengths between them.

data.text: The algorithm takes an original graph as input and produces the minimum-time path covering all vertices. It creates a complete time-weighted graph by adding hypothetical edges and replacing distances with travel times, then uses a standard travelling salesman problem solver to find the optimal path. This path is post-processed to replace hypothetical edges with original shortest paths, though the final time may still exceed cybersickness thresholds in large environments.
points: The algorithm takes an original graph as input and produces the minimum-time path covering all vertices.
It creates a complete time-weighted graph by adding hypothetical edges and replacing distances with travel times.
A standard travelling salesman problem solver finds the optimal time and path, which is then post-processed by replacing hypothetical edges with original shortest paths.
The final time may still exceed cybersickness thresholds in large environments.

data.text: Cybersickness can be minimized by either finding the minimum-time path to cover all points of interest or maximizing points covered within a fixed time limit. The minimum-time approach maps the virtual world to a graph and solves it as a travelling salesman problem (TSP) using walking speed models. While hypothetical edges are removed to produce the final path, the travel time might still exceed the threshold for cybersickness.
points: There are two approaches to minimize cybersickness: finding a minimum-time path for all points of interest or finding the maximum points within a time limit.
The minimum-time approach represents the virtual world as a graph where nodes are points of interest.
This travel problem is solved as a travelling salesman problem (TSP) using travel times from a natural walking speed model.
Hypothetical edges are removed from the final path, though the travel time may still exceed the threshold for cybersickness.
